subtype: Approach: tracking progress with a chart [Action]
passage: My name is Alka, and learning to skate felt slower than a snail. Some weeks I fell more than I glided. Coach Kamal said, "Mark a star on your calendar each day you practise." So I stuck one on my wall, and after every session, helmet and pads on, I drew a gold star. On bad days I still drew the star, even if I had only rolled to the gate and back. By the third week there was a row of stars like a fence. When I felt like quitting I looked at the row and thought, that is a lot of showing up. Last Sunday I did a full turn without putting a hand down.

qa.q: Who suggested putting a star on the calendar?
How did the row of stars make Alka feel when feeling like quitting?
qa.a: Alka felt encouraged, because the row was proof of a lot of showing up even when progress felt slow.

qa.q: What could Alka add to the chart to see skill as well as effort?
qa.a: Write one thing learned beside each star, because it shows improvement and not just the number of days.

qa.q: How might Coach Kamal see the calendar?
qa.a: As a helpful sign of regular practice, since the coach can see the effort at a glance.

grounding: A learner marks a star for each practice day, and the growing row keeps Alka going through slow weeks.

passage:
Coach's note, Sunday batch, lakeside skating rink
Hemant has been coming for six weeks now. In week three he told me he wanted to quit because he still couldn't glide without flapping his arms. His mother mentioned the calendar he keeps at home: a gold star for every practice day. I asked him to bring it. Today he did. Twenty-one stars in a row, a few smudged. He ran his finger along them and said, "That's a lot of stars for someone who can't skate." Then he laughed. His arms are still wobbly, but he did two full laps without grabbing the rail. I have told him we'll add a silver star the day he stops flapping.
— Vidya, coach

qa.q: How many stars were on Hemant's calendar?
qa.a: There were twenty-one stars in a row, a few smudged.

qa.q: Why did Hemant laugh when he ran his finger along the stars?
qa.a: He seemed pleased and a bit surprised to see how much practice he had done even when he felt he couldn't skate, which lifted his discouragement.

qa.q: What else could keep Hemant going through slow weeks?
qa.a: Small skill markers like the silver star for no flapping, so he sees progress in skill as well as in days practised.

qa.q: How does Vidya see the calendar?
qa.a: Vidya treats it as proof of Hemant's steady effort, useful enough to ask him to bring it and to add a new kind of star.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy's row of practice stars keeping him going through slow weeks of learning to skate.

passage:
Thursday night
Fell twice today at the society rink. Scraped the same knee as last week. Came home cross and said I was done with skates forever. Then I saw the calendar on my cupboard door. Eighteen stars since the holidays began, one for every practice day, and I drew each one myself. My sister Mehak said, "If you stop now, the row stops too." That annoyed me because it was true. Mummy said, "Kal dekhte hain, beta," and got me ice for the knee. After dinner I went down again for ten minutes, just going round the edge slowly. Came back up and drew star number nineteen. It's a wobbly star. Still counts.
Sahil

qa.a: Sahil fell twice at the society rink.

qa.q: Why was Sahil annoyed at what Mehak said?
qa.a: Sahil felt cross and discouraged after the falls, and was annoyed because Mehak was right that stopping would break the row of stars.

qa.q: What might help Sahil on days when skating feels slow?
qa.a: A short, easy session like ten minutes round the edge, just enough to earn the star, keeps the habit alive without pushing too hard.

qa.q: What is it like for Mehak to see Sahil come home cross?
qa.a: Mehak may feel concerned but wants to encourage him, using the star row to nudge him without nagging.

grounding: A boy's diary shows the growing row of calendar stars pulling him back to skating on a discouraging day.
